I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01129

Certainly, one may ask how he is present. Sayyed Haydar recalls the case of Khezr (Khadîr), of Elijah carried away in a chariot of fire, and of Jesus taken up by God while the Jews believed they were crucifying him. History also records cases of extraordinary longevity extending over centuries. We may observe that these last examples perhaps do not really meet the difficulty; closer to the point are those Shiite writers who invoke the idea of a world parallel to our own, the world of Hûrqalyâ. What especially draws our attention, however, is the way all these arguments of Haydar Âmolî converge at one point: the point where reasoning gives way to an appeal to direct testimony.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01130

Shiite theory of knowledge permits this, since it extends the possibility of inspired knowledge (ilhâm), whether visionary or not, throughout the entire cycle of walâyat. This is why, in Mollâ Sadrâ, the theory of the Active Imagination as the spiritual faculty attuned to the imaginal world acquires such importance. Haydar Âmolî's visions directly perceive the unity of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in the fullness of their eternal reality. Through these visions he is raised to the status of an eyewitness (shâhid), able to testify that the Muhammadan imamate is the Seal of walâyat.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01131

Our Sayyed recounts three personal visions. The first two are explicitly dated, though he does not relate them in chronological order; we shall, of course, keep the order he chose. The first vision in his account came to him in Baghdad in 755/1354. The second, as he tells the story, had occurred seven years earlier while he was in Khorassan, in eastern Iran.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01132

The third is undated. He was then at Karbala, at the shrine of the Third Imam, Hosayn ibn ’Alî, the “Prince of Martyrs.” Think for a moment of what the star-filled sky over Baghdad or Khorassan can look like. The clarity of the air brings it so near that you feel you could reach out and touch the stars. Their brilliance suggests a perfect text, but one written in signs or letters whose key has been lost. Certain mystics, such as Najmoddin Kobrâ (d. 1220), have been able to decipher these “books written in Heaven.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01133

But our Sayyed's visions were so clear that he had nothing to decipher. Each time the same sequence unfolds. A configuration appears in the sky; its meaning is given by the voice of an unseen presence, without the angel appearing. This is entirely consistent with Shiite theory of knowledge.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01134

The mystic first sees luminous diagrams symbolizing the Fourteen Immaculate Ones, then the triad from which they originate, and finally the Five who, despite the equality of all fourteen, hold a privileged position among them. At the end of his account, the author specifies that he contemplated the first vision “on the surface of the first heaven,” in its northeastern region, and the second in its northwestern region. The detail is significant: Baghdad lies to the west, Khorassan to the east, and the positions of the two visions therefore converge upon the pole.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01135

1) Of the first vision, then, Haydar Âmolî tells us that it was granted to him in Baghdad in 755/1354. In relating the second, he will clarify that he was not dreaming but awake, which therefore points to the intermediate state of perception. He does not give the hour, but the figures he describes could only have been perceived, even imaginally, in the night sky. In the third account, indeed, he will explicitly mention the starry heavens.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01136

Sayyed Haydar was standing east of Baghdad, in the Ra’s al-Yarr quarter, opposite a theological school called the Madrasa moghithîya. He was looking toward the northern sky—or, more precisely, as he later explains, the northeast. There he saw a square figure with fourteen circles touching its sides or corners, some lying inside and some outside its perimeter. The memory remained so precise that he reproduced the figure exactly in the introduction to his commentary on the Fosûs. We need only describe it, following the details he himself gives in the text.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01137

The circles were inscribed with the names of the Twelve Imams—or, more precisely, of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. The author explains that, seen from one perspective, the Immaculate Ones number twelve, while from another they number fourteen. The Twelve Imams, as the inward dimension (walâyat) of the eternal Muhammadan Reality or Light, form the complete company of Fourteen together with the Prophet, who represents its outward prophetic dimension (nobowwat), and Fâtima, his daughter and the mother of their line. Fâtima is the point at which the two Lights meet: the light of prophecy and the light of walâyat.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01138

Another remarkable detail brings out the contrast of blue and gold that characterizes the vision: the names of the Fourteen were written in red gold upon circles each made of lapis lazuli (Persian lazhovard).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01139

The arrangement of the names is equally striking. The four circles placed outside the four corners of the square bear the names of the four figures within this eternal company who share the name Mohammad. Starting at the upper right and proceeding around the figure, they are Mohammad the Prophet; the Fifth Imam, Mohammad al-Bâqir; the Ninth Imam, Mohammad al-Javâd al-Taqî; and the Twelfth Imam, Mohammad al-Mahdî (compare the list of the Twelve in Book I, Chapter II). The four circles set inside the four corners of the square bear the names of those who share the name ’Alî: the First Imam, ’Alî Mortazâ; the Fourth, ’Alî Zayn al-’Abidîn; the Eighth, ’Alî Rezâ; and the Tenth, ’Alî Naqî. Along the vertical centerline are four symmetrically arranged circles.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01140

At the top, outside the square, the circle of Fâtima the Radiant, the Prophet's daughter and the source of the Imams' lineage, presides over the entire figure (compare the first vision of Mîr Dâmâd, infra, Book VI, Chapter I). Touching her circle, within the square, is that of the Second Imam, Hasan al-Mojtabâ. At the bottom, inside the square, is the circle of the Sixth Imam, Ja’far al-Sâdiq; outside it is the circle of the Eleventh Imam, Hasan al-’Askarî.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01141

Finally, at the “east” and “west” of the figure, on its horizontal centerline and within the square's perimeter, are the circles bearing respectively the names of the Third Imam, Hosayn, the martyr of Karbala, and the Seventh, Mûsâ al-Kâzem—the only two in the eternal company to bear their respective names. The arrangement of the Fourteen thus gives the diagram an intelligible structure. The large central circle is filled with closely packed writing, which explains that the figure of this vision is reproduced here as testimony against Ibn ’Arabî's doctrine that Jesus is the Seal of walâyat.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01142

The writing then repeats the distinctive features and circumstances of the vision, duplicating what is already said on the page. In truth, it would have been better to leave this central circle empty. It could then symbolize, more fittingly, the inaccessible center of divine Oneness, approached from afar only through a theology that speaks of God by denying the limits of all descriptions, while the Fourteen arranged around it would represent the forms in which the divine appears.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01143

Our Sayyed remains absorbed in contemplation of this wonderful arrangement. “The universe,” he writes, “was illuminated by the light of these circles and figures. The people were reciting aloud the prayer of blessing upon the Prophet and the members of his House, and I was doing the same. Then, while I was in this state, I heard a voice coming from heaven, the voice of an unseen being, saying to me: These are the ones who, after their forefather (the Prophet), are the goal toward which being (wojûd) and the manifestation of being (zohûr) tend. They are those called the Poles (Aqtâb), the Substitutes (Abdâl), the Pillars (Awtâd), and the Solitaries (Afrâd).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01144

“Through them walâyat is sealed in both its universal and its particular senses, just as prophecy, in its universal and particular senses, was brought to a close through their forefather. They are his representatives (kholafâ) on earth and in heaven. Through the last of them, the twelfth, who is the Mahdî, particular Muhammadan walâyat is sealed. Through him the Hour will dawn, and at his death this world will be transformed into the world beyond.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01145
Diagram drawn by Haydar Âmolî of his vision in the night sky over Baghdad, 755/1354 (Istanbul manuscript, Carullah 1470, fol. 49b).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01146
The Fourteen Immaculate Ones (the Prophet, Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams)
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01149
Our Sayyed reminds us that he has explained all this several times in his books.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01150

But because the argument is directed against Ibn ’Arabî's interpretation of the Seal of walâyat, he also recalls that the eminent shaykh himself described this mystery of the Twelve in his own writings. Ibn ’Arabî explained clearly that God created twelve Angels in the eighth heaven and made that heaven their dwelling place. The twelve “towers,” or signs of the zodiac, symbolize their respective abodes there, and the names of these lofty towers are the Angels' names. Ibn ’Arabî knows perfectly well that the twelve Noqabâ (chiefs), the twelve tribes of Israel, and the twelve Imams are the forms in which they appear. It is from these primordial Angels that the twelve receive the spiritual influence which they in turn pour out upon created beings. Sayyed Haydar leaves a fuller explanation for another occasion.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01151

2) The second vision our author relates had come to him seven years earlier, in 748/1347. He mentions in passing that serious epidemics broke out that year, lasting two years and devastating human and animal populations alike, from Khorassan through Persian Iraq and into Arab Iraq. He tells us that he himself was in eastern Iran, in Khorassan, without specifying the place. He was still at the beginning of his spiritual practice (fî ibtidâ’ al-tajrîd). He also stresses that the vision came while he was awake.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01152

As in the previous account, Sayyed Haydar is standing and contemplating the northern region of the sky—or more precisely, as he shortly explains, the northwest. He sees a perfectly rectangular geometric figure inscribed in the heavens. He gives its approximate dimensions, as best he could judge them: ten cubits by four. Here again the figure is traced in lapis lazuli, while the names it bears are written in letters of gold.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01153

The repetition of this combination of colors is significant. This time there are three names: Allâh, Mohammad, and ’Alî. They are arranged so that the m (mîm) of Mohammad corresponds to the h (hâ) of Allâh, and the ’ayn of ’Alî corresponds to the d (dâl) of Mohammad. Meanwhile, the curve of the final letter of ’Alî's name—the yâ—extends into a flourish that sweeps back beneath the name and joins the initial alef of Allâh, so that the two names become a single composition, a single form. The details of this description are not entirely clear, and unfortunately the author did not draw the figure. We offer a sketch below, in the hope that it corresponds more or less to what our Sayyed saw.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01155

As in the preceding account, he relates that the whole universe shone with the radiance of this figure and of the names inscribed upon it. The people were engaged in the prayer of blessing upon the Prophet and the members of his House, and he was doing the same. He questioned someone present, but received the reply: “We do not know the secret of this.” Once again, he heard an unseen voice speaking very loudly from the heights of heaven:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01156

“The secret is that you, and both worlds, should know through direct experience that all existence revolves around these three. For they are the form of God (sûrat al-Haqq ta’âlâ), the form of His outward aspect (zâhir) and the form of His inward reality (sûrat bâtinî-hi).”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01157

Sayyed Haydar then explains the meaning of the declaration made by the unseen voice. In essence, the three names of light inscribed within the lapis-lazuli rectangle express the secret of the eternal Muhammadan Reality (Haqîqat mohammadiya), understood as the complete, primordial manifestation of God. Allah is the supreme Name of the revealed God, the Deus revelatus. When this God revealed and manifested Himself in the eternal Muhammadan Reality, He assigned its inward aspect to universal or absolute walâyat—the bond of divine friendship and spiritual guardianship—and to the absolute Friend of God (walî motlaq), the Imam. Its outward aspect He assigned to universal prophecy and to the Prophet who is its Seal.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01158
Thus the manifestation of God, and the manifestation of being itself, revolves around this triad.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01159

“The three Essences [to which the three names in the figure refer] are the essential Reality of the Real (Haqîqat al-Haqq), its inward aspect, and its outward aspect. Only through these three together does the structure of existence take shape, and all beings are forms in which they appear and become manifest. Just as universal prophecy embraces the manifestations of Muhammad—the outward aspect of the Muhammadan Reality—namely, the prophets and messengers whose Seal is Muhammad, so universal walâyat embraces the manifestations of Ali—the inward aspect of the Muhammadan Reality—namely, the awliyâ’, all the Friends of God and the perfected beings whose Seal is the Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01160
“Hence the famous saying of the Prophet: God sent Ali secretly with every prophet; with me, He sent him openly.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01161

As Haydar Amoli himself understands it, this vision brings together everything we discussed earlier (Book I). The diagram shining in the heavens encodes the secret of the metaphysics of being, which cannot be separated from “prophetic philosophy.” Whenever we read his discussions of being and its manifestation, we must therefore keep in mind their connection with his visionary experience. Imamology—the understanding of the Imams—is woven into ontology, the understanding of being, and ontology into Imamology. This was a powerful philosophical construction, but it was not what we might nowadays dismiss as a mere intellectual speculation. It rested on the testimony of direct vision, on an actual entry into worlds beyond the reach of the senses.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01162

The stroke of writing connecting the Imam’s name to that of the Deus revelatus indicates that the Imamate—that is, walâyat, divine friendship or nearness—is both the origin and the culmination of God's manifestation. It is the reason that manifestation occurs and the form in which it is fulfilled, because walî, the protecting Friend, is one of the divine Names par excellence. Earlier, the idea of walâyat had already led us to recognize Shiism as a form of the religion of spiritual love (Book I, Chapter VII). A third visionary account by Haydar Amoli completes the preceding two and offers moving confirmation of this insight.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01163

Every Shiite spiritual seeker thinks of Salman the Pure as an archetype whose experience he seeks to repeat in his own life. The Imam's words to Salman—“You are one of us, a member of the Prophet’s House”—are words that Sayyed Haydar will now hear addressed to himself. This happens in another vision, the third in the sequence of his account. 3) This time, Sayyed Haydar is at Karbala, the very place where the Third Imam, Husayn ibn Ali, was martyred, and where his revered sanctuary stands. He does not specify the year, but he implies that the vision came after many other experiences, and therefore later than the two already described.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01164

What he sees now is neither the entire company of the blazing names of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones who constitute the heavenly pleroma—the fullness of sacred beings—nor the names of the triad from which that fullness originates. Instead, he sees five privileged names from among that company: those known as the “People of the Cloak.” The name refers to the famous episode of the mubâhala, the proposed ordeal of mutual imprecation between the Prophet and the Christians of Najran, including their bishop, from which the Christians withdrew at the last moment.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01165

The Prophet had come with his own family, “with his souls,” sheltering them beneath his cloak, which was stretched between two poles against the backdrop of the desert. It is these five names that Haydar Amoli sees written in letters of white light upon emerald tablets. We are reminded here of the emerald tablet possessed by Fatima, upon which the names of the Twelve Imams were inscribed. Muhammad al-Baqir, the Fifth Imam, once showed it to his close disciple Jabir al-Ansari. As in the preceding accounts, Sayyed Haydar is absorbed in contemplation of the starry sky, like someone trying to decipher the lines of writing traced by the constellations.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01166

“I was standing in the courtyard [of the sanctuary], contemplating the sky and its stars. Someone unseen said to me: ‘Read—or recite—the lines you see written there.’ Then I saw lines written in white light upon emerald tablets. They were the supreme Name of God together with the names of the Five Blessed Ones among His Friends and intimates: Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01167

“Then the unseen voice said to me: ‘These are the very essence of existence and the purpose of God. They are the Words through which God turned toward Adam and accepted his repentance. And it is through them that God accepts your own return to Him, for you are one of their number [like Salman]. You belong among those who are objects of God's love, those of whom He said: “God will bring forth people who love Him and whom He loves” (2:59).’”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01168

This Qur'anic verse contains the whole idea of walâyat (Persian dûstî) as friendship with God and love for God. The Imam is its pole and its Seal, because he is the form in which the inward reality of the Muhammadan Reality becomes manifest—the form around which this love is centered.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01169

“Then,” Sayyed Haydar continues, “I returned to myself, filled with intense joy and gladness. I thanked God for all of this, and for the many things that had repeatedly happened to me, but which this is not the place to recount.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01170

It was important to make these three visions known here. Without them, our understanding of a Shiite spiritual thinker as representative as Haydar Amoli would remain incomplete. For him, as for the Shaykh al-Ishrâq—Suhrawardi, the master of the philosophy of Illumination—philosophical knowledge is directed toward personal spiritual realization. In Suhrawardi’s case, this realization culminates in visions of pure beings of light, the Perfect Nature, and other such presences.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01171

In Haydar Amoli’s case, it is the vision of the heavenly fullness of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones: “persons of light” who together constitute one and the same light, the Muhammadan Light (Nûr mohammadî). This is not a merely figurative vision. It is symbolic in the fullest sense: their names blaze in the depths of the starry heavens. For both Suhrawardi and Haydar Amoli, such personal experience of sacred knowledge is irrefutable testimony, evidence more compelling than any philosophical or theological demonstration based on dialectical reasoning or the authority of transmitted traditions.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01172

Yet Sayyed Haydar does not lose sight of the question at issue in this chapter—the question that prompted him to recount his visions in the first place. It concerns the Seal of walâyat in the person of the Twelfth Imam.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01173

“That is why,” he says, “I have recounted these visions here, principally as testimony to counterbalance the dream of Ibn Arabi.” He means the dream Ibn Arabi had interpreted as referring simply to himself, rather than to the Seal of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01174

Haydar Amoli considers that he has fully accomplished his task on this point. He believes he has given “prophetic philosophy” the threefold philosophical, theological, and theosophical foundation he had set out to establish. Much was at stake. The reference to the “Words that interceded for Adam” brings into full view the relationship between the understanding of Adam and the understanding of the Imams, and therefore between Adam's transgression and the saving role of the Imams. The Imam is called the “Adam of the awliyâ’,” the Friends of God.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01175

Ibn Arabi had disrupted this relationship by transferring to Jesus a designation which, once the cycle of prophecy had closed, could belong only to the Imamate of the Twelve. Here is a point of fundamental importance for any future comparative theology, one that has so far gone entirely unnoticed. The issue is how Shiite theologians understand Adam's transgression, something we have already touched upon.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01176
Let us therefore conclude by quoting a few more lines from Haydar Amoli, a hadith recorded on the last page of the same chapter of his introduction to his commentary on the Fosûs:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01177

“When God wished to turn again toward Adam [toward humanity], He said to him: ‘Contemplate the heavens.’ Adam looked, and the veil was lifted before him as far as the supports of the Throne. He saw written upon the Throne, in letters of light, the names of the Five Persons: Muhammad, Ali, Fatima, Hasan, and Husayn. He cried out: ‘My God! What are these names? Have You created other beings before me?’ ‘No,’ came the reply. ‘These are your descendants and your children.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01178

“But if I created you, if I created the universe, it was for their sake and because of them. Recite their Names, so that through their blessed influence I may turn toward you again.’ Then Adam recited their Names, and God turned toward him. These are the Words mentioned in the Qur'an (2:35), which God taught Adam in order to accept his repentance.”
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01179

The “Five People of the Cloak” present at the mubâhala were also the Five whom the angel Gabriel considered it an honor to join as a “sixth.” This occurred when Gabriel appeared on the day the verse was revealed that consecrates the earthly persons of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones:
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01180
“God wishes only to remove all impurity from you, O People of My House (ahl al-bayt), and to make you utterly pure” (33:33).
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01181

On this verse, as on the verse concerning the Words that interceded for Adam, Haydar Amoli can appeal to the agreement of all Shiite commentators. The Imam, the Perfect Human Being, is the ultimate purpose of creation, the secret of cosmology and salvation, the redeemer of Adam. We know that Sayyed Haydar had reflected particularly deeply on the meaning of Adam's transgression: the paradox of a sublime error, an act of daring that was bound to turn against Adam and his descendants, because his powers were not equal to the burden he had agreed to bear. That was paradise lost. With the cycle of walâyat, following the cycle of prophecy, the return to paradise regained begins.
I. Haydar Amoli, a Shiite Theologian of Sufism
passage-en-01182

And the form of this return corresponds to the distinctive character of Shiite mysticism, at once theosophical and ecstatic. This is not an ecstasy that seeks to extinguish the world and the self by immersion in the divine current. Theosophical wisdom opens the way to vision. And visionary experience is, above all, the joy of being-with: being with the one and the beings who, for the mystic, give form to love.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01183
Chapter II An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
en-book-4-ch-2-s1
1. Interpretation and the Types of Spiritual Seekers
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01184

The chapters that follow will, in effect, develop more fully the themes introduced at the beginning of this work (Book I, Chapters IV and V), and taken up again in our discussion of Haydar Amoli, whose writings have shown us the importance of interpreting the Qur'an's inner meanings.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01185

We shall first examine an anonymous Persian treatise from the eighth/fourteenth century. It offers an excellent Sufi interpretation of the celebrated hadith affirming that the Qur'an possesses seven inner meanings.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01186

We shall then turn to a ninth/fifteenth-century treatise by Sa'inoddin Torkeh Isfahani, a Shiite author of exceptional intellectual depth. His work is, in a sense, a practical exercise in interpreting the inner meaning of a Qur'anic verse. It shows how this method of interpretation gives rise to a classification of different spiritual types.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01187

Finally, returning to the preceding century, we shall give particular attention to the major work of Alaoddawleh Semnani (d. 736/1336). In Semnani we shall find the same conviction as in Sa'inoddin Torkeh: every way of understanding expresses a corresponding way of being, from which that understanding arises and upon which it depends. For both thinkers, interpretation therefore develops in relation to a spiritual typology—or, more precisely, through the discovery of the kinds of spiritual seekers to whom the successive levels of interpretation correspond. By connecting the organs of subtle spiritual physiology with the stages of interpreting hidden meaning, Semnani carried the inward appropriation of Revelation and the doctrine of prophecy to their furthest possible point.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01188

Step by step, he leads the mystic to reproduce inwardly the experience of the Prophet. The meaning of the supreme shari'a revealed to the mystic on his own “Sinai”—that is, at the summit of his soul—is the religion of the “supreme prophet of his own being.” It is a genuinely personal religion that supersedes all others, because the Sufi measures their lateness not against the history of the world, but against the history of his own being.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01189

Before examining the methods required for this ever-deepening interpretation of inner meaning, let us consider how, as recently as the preceding century, the distinguished Iranian Shiite theosopher Ja'far Kashfi summarized the function and task of spiritual interpretation. His explanations would be enough, if any reminder were needed, to show how radically this approach differs from allegorical interpretation.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01190

But they also reveal the same concern that we have encountered in the authors just mentioned: the desire to establish a relationship between levels of interpretation and types of spiritual seekers. In this respect, these Iranian thinkers anticipated questions that are now associated with what we call “philosophical anthropology.” Ja'far Kashfi relates the different levels of interpretation to different kinds of philosopher and different forms of philosophy. Interpretation in general, he says, has three levels: tafsîr, ta’wîl, and tafhîm.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01191

Tafsîr, the interpretation of the literal text, is a discipline centered on the established Islamic religious sciences. It also requires a sound knowledge of the relevant literature. Its concern is exclusively with what the text explicitly says. It represents the lowest level of knowledge and learning. Ta’wîl literally means “to lead back” or “to return” something to its origin, principle, or archetype. The term is commonly used for any symbolic interpretation, as distinct from tafsîr. This form of knowledge depends on spiritual guidance and divine assistance. When intention, capacity, effective help, and attainment of the goal all come together, happiness is complete. It represents the middle level of knowledge and of those who possess it.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01192

Finally, tafhîm literally means “to make someone understand.” Here it designates interpretation in the deeper, technical sense that concerns us. It is a form of knowledge centered on an act of Understanding (fahm) through God, and on an inspiration (ilhâm) of which God is at once the subject, the object, and the goal—or, equivalently, the source, the means, and the end. This is the highest level of knowledge and of those who possess it. The knowledge proper to ta’wîl is an intuitive unveiling, a penetration of meaning through inner vision (kashf). The knowledge proper to tafhîm is divine inspiration.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01193

If we wish to relate these three levels of interpretation to three levels of philosophical wisdom, our author explains, we must first say that tafsîr involves no philosophy (hikmat) at all. If we nevertheless insist on drawing a parallel, it would correspond to the philosophy of the Peripatetics. The knowledge of ta’wîl corresponds to the philosophy of the Stoics (hikmat al-Rawâq), because it is a wisdom concerned with what lies behind the Veil (hijâb; rawâq = stoa, a portico). The knowledge of tafhîm—interpretation in its truest sense, or transcendent interpretation—is “Oriental” or Illuminationist wisdom (hikmat al-Ishrâq) as Suhrawardi understood it (see Book II).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01194

We shall encounter the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of Illumination, again in this very discussion (Chapter III), where they are assigned this elevated place. That alone would be enough to demonstrate the influence exerted over the centuries by this “Oriental” theosophy. Since Suhrawardi, it has maintained a continuous tradition linking ancient Persia with Islamic Iran.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01195

We can immediately see how Ja'far Kashfi's Shiite conception of interpretation gives expression to concerns that arise wherever a sacred Book is experienced not simply as material for philological research—the province of tafsîr—but as a source of spiritual life. Understood in this way, the “phenomenon of the Book” extends beyond the limits traditionally associated with the Ahl al-Kitâb, the People of the Book. It appears wherever a book can be read in the way that one reads the Bible or the Qur'an.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01196

The Mathnawî of Jalaloddin Rumi, that immense poetic composition devoted to the symbols of the soul, is studied and lived as the “Persian Qur'an” (Qorân-e fârsî). Hafiz's Dîwân is still used daily by Sufis in Iran as one might use the Bible. We know the remarkable interpretation of the Odyssey developed by the Pythagoreans. Likewise, the later Neoplatonists, such as Proclus, practiced a fully developed ta’wîl upon the traditions handed down from the ancient Greek “theologians.” For them, too, the successive levels of interpretation corresponded to a hierarchy of spiritual types.

2. The Eternal Event of the Book
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01197

Let us now examine the first of the short treatises announced above. As we have already mentioned, the manuscript preserving this little work in Persian—so far the only known copy—does not give its author's name. The copy is dated 731/1331, exactly five years before the death of Semnani (736/1336), whose spiritual interpretation we shall examine below. It also dates from the period of Sayyed Haydar Amoli's youth.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01198

Both its vocabulary and its contents suggest that the copy was made not very long after the unknown author lived. The treatise is a commentary on a fundamental hadith to which we have already had occasion to refer. The author shows how the seven inner meanings of the Qur'an correspond to a hierarchy of seven levels of spiritual understanding. The same idea will appear in the classification of spiritual seekers developed by Sa'inoddin Torkeh (Chapter III below).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01199

“There is,” our anonymous author writes, “a saying attributed by tradition to the Prophet (hadîth nabawî) upon which I have meditated deeply and conducted a careful investigation. I plunged into the ocean of the Qur'an's secrets and brought forth the pearls of its subtleties.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01200

“I lifted the veils of sounds and letters from before its true Realities (haqâ’iq), the hidden meanings kept beyond human sight. This hadith declares that the Qur'an possesses an outward meaning and an inward meaning. In other words, it has a zâhir—a back or outward surface, the literal meaning—and a bâtin—an inward depth, like a womb, the hidden or spiritual meaning. And this inward meaning itself has an inward meaning: one depth contains another, as the celestial spheres are nested within one another. So it continues, down to seven inward meanings, seven depths within depths.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01201

This hadith, then, proposes a progressive deepening of Qur'anic understanding through seven levels. Before showing that these seven levels correspond precisely to the seven levels of spiritual seekers—because each degree of understanding corresponds to a distinct way of being, an inner state—the author considers it necessary to take a position on two questions that govern the entire study of the Qur'an.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01202

As we have emphasized at length, these questions arise directly from the phenomenon of the sacred Book itself (see Book I, Chapter IV). They therefore confront every religious community whose life is centered on a revealed Book, a text proclaimed by a Nâtiq, a prophetic speaker. The first question is this: what is the relationship between a revealed text, expressed in a particular language at a particular moment, and the eternal truth that it communicates?
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01203

The second concerns the very process of revelation. How are we to understand it? In other words, do we possess a psychology of prophecy capable of explaining the passage from the divine Word to its human expression? The first question leads us back to the fundamental controversy that, because it was wrongly framed, threw the early Islamic community into turmoil: Is the Qur'an created or uncreated? The question was wrongly framed because the two alternatives do not refer to the same thing.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01204

Unfortunately, recognizing this requires a minimum of philosophical understanding—something the political authorities scarcely possessed as they successively imposed one position and then the other. It is equally clear that the problem goes far beyond the assumptions and resources of critical philology. For the philologist, the Qur'anic text as we read it appears to be historically conditioned. Its natural meaning must therefore, in the philologist's view, be reconstructed from the historical circumstances of a particular religious environment.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01205

But for our author, as for all those who share his approach, the true meaning of the Qur'an cannot be confined to the external circumstances surrounding the letter of the text. Their demands are precisely what have led us to formulate the problem of interpretation in its full rigor.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01206

Moreover, the variety of possible meanings depends on the spiritual development of the reader, whoever that reader may be—including the Western philologist who encounters the Qur'an at some particular moment in historical time. If the philologist decides that the true meaning is the natural, philological meaning of the words, that very decision places him, by virtue of his spiritual state, among the exoteric interpreters: those who remain at the level of outward appearances. No one escapes the strict law of this situation of interpretation.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01207

The same law applies when we turn to the second question, that of prophetic psychology. The Western interpreter seeks to understand a prophet by studying his environment, education, or particular genius. The Sufi interpreter seeks to understand him by meditating upon the nature of his relationship with the eternal Source from which his message proceeds—the Revelation whose text he proclaims. The psychology of the prophet is therefore an essential part of the doctrine of prophecy.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01208

Every philosopher and every theosopher within Sufism is concerned with it. And the fact that each individual takes responsibility for this question is itself a sign of a community founded upon the authority of the Book alone, and upon every believer's personal relationship with that Book and the meaning it possesses for that believer's own existence. Such a community is not founded upon the authority of a teaching institution that determines what meaning the sacred text must have according to a doctrine whose development it controls.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01209

Our author deals with both questions in a short prologue. Through his mystical theosophy, he escapes not only the dilemma posed by the theologians of Kalâm, but also the dilemma that a modern philosopher might put to him: How can truth be historical, and how can history be truth?
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01210

“Know,” he writes, “and may God come to your aid and ours through a Spirit proceeding from Him, that the eternal essence (haqîqat) of the Qur'an is the divine Logos or Word (Kalâm-e Haqq). It abides with and through the divine Selfhood, inseparable from it, without beginning or end in eternity. This is what the verse indicates: ‘It is We who have sent down the Reminder (dhikr), and it is We who preserve it’ (15:9). The Divine Being speaks a single Word that never changes, although languages, technical terms, and forms of expression differ.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01211

This Word is not even conditioned by whether the world exists or does not exist. For the world is not a reality existing outside God. Creation is a manifestation of God; it is not the coming into existence of something separate from, and alongside, the Divine Being. Here our author agrees with all the Sufis of Ibn Arabi's school. The saying “God was, and there was nothing with Him” must therefore immediately be qualified by another: “And it is still now as it has always been.” One objection can easily be anticipated.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01212

If the divine Word is eternal, and if the events it reveals are consequently eternal as well, what becomes of the very notion of an event? How, for example, can we imagine that, in pre-eternity, when the Prophet had not yet appeared and the unbelievers still lay hidden behind the veil of nonbeing or nonmanifestation, God could have said to him: “O Prophet, struggle against the unbelievers” (9:74)? And how can we conceive, without absurdity, that Moses, before he had even entered into existence, could have said to God, “Show Yourself to me, so that I may behold You,” and received the reply, “You shall not see Me” (7:139)? The Sufi master's answer rests on one consideration alone: this entire objection is illusory, because it depends on a completely mistaken way of imagining the matter.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01213

The illusion arises from a confusion between different kinds of time. It is precisely this confusion that Semnani avoids by distinguishing, in technical terms, between zamân âfâqî, the time of the objective world—the quantitative, continuous time of history—and zamân anfusî, the inward time of the soul, which is purely qualitative. Before and after presuppose a uniform, continuous, irreversible time, measurable by the revolutions of the heavenly bodies.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01214

But an event that takes place within the soul, in the soul's own time, cannot, in what essentially constitutes it, be situated before or after some particular calendar date. Such a date does not determine it. The event does not belong to the history of the world, “beneath the horizons of the world.” As we have said before, neither theophanies—manifestations of God—nor their visionary events can be turned into ordinary objective history or historical time. Visionary events possess their own time, whose relation to measurable calendar time is expressed in the verse:
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01215
“One day with your Lord is like a thousand of the years that you count” (22:46).
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01216

To say that a day is equivalent to a millennium is to say that there is no rational common measure between the qualitative time of the soul and the quantitative time of worldly history. It would be equally mistaken to imagine the moments “with your Lord” as mathematical points without duration. Even that description would smuggle in a quantitative idea, if only by denying it. There is indeed an eternal duration. There are “days with your Lord.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01217

But none of our methods of reckoning time can measure them. These are the days of eternal events. It is therefore absurd to ask how Moses could have said this or that “before he existed.” It is precisely because such a question is absurd that the revealed text possesses both an outward, apparent meaning and an inward, hidden meaning. The inward meaning is spiritual, but it is not an allegory. It is a higher order of reality, grounded in the relationship through which the invisible becomes manifest. If we fail to understand this, we can find reality only on the plane of history.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01218

But then the phenomena of history cease to be phenomena in the full sense, because they no longer disclose any spiritual meaning. To search for that meaning is to give events a dimension they cannot possess within a conception of history that regards its own continuous unfolding as sufficient to provide it with meaning. Our anonymous Sufi declares:
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01219

“Whoever has once risen above the world of material objects, freeing himself from the narrow passage of nights and days, and turns resolutely toward the world of the soul, drawing time and place inward, will become aware that the divine world knows no before or after or now, no alteration and no passing from one form to another.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01220

“At this level of being, this divine ‘Presence’ (hazrat), one must not imagine any extension measurable by our standards, not even the extension of an atom or a point. This is what is meant when we say that, by the reckoning of the gnostics, a thousand years are equal to the blink of an eye, or to a flash of lightning that bursts forth in the Orient of divinity. Then one becomes aware that, for the Divine Being, the Qur'an is the Word uttered through His own breath, His divine Exhalation. It embraces pre-eternity and post-eternity. It is not a new event that comes into being when the person to whom it is addressed finally appears.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01221

Thus the phenomenon of the Book—its visible, outward appearance (zâhir)—is led back to its eternal archetype. The Book in its outward form is not merely paper and ink. It consists of readable words, audible sounds, and apparent meanings accessible to human understanding.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01222

Yet behind this form lies the “Mother of the Book” (Omm al-Kitâb), the eternal divine Word concealed beneath its outward covering. This is what establishes the legitimacy of ta’wîl: the spiritual practice of leading the literal form of every Revelation back to its inward meaning. Our author freely acknowledges the difficulty.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01223

“Know,” he says, “that this is one of the most obscure questions in the whole of theosophical wisdom. One cannot understand it by accumulating rational arguments and proofs. But if there is a receptive soul, possessing at least some measure of inward purity and endowed with a mystical sensitivity to spiritual realities, then it is possible for that soul to understand.”
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01224

However difficult it may be to understand the sacred Book in relation to its archetype, the eternal divine Word, this very relationship supplies the answer to the second preliminary question. How can that divine Word “pass through” the language of the successive prophets entrusted with proclaiming it? This question belongs simultaneously to the study of prophecy, the study of angels, and psychology. It has concerned philosophers and theologians alike. We have already encountered it at the very origins of Shiism.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01225

For what a psychology of prophecy must explain, if it is to account for the sacred Book, is the passage from inward to outward meaning brought about by revelation through the prophet (tanzîl), and the return from outward to inward meaning accomplished through spiritual interpretation (ta’wîl). Our author confines himself to a brief outline of the essentials. He presupposes the notion of the “holy intellect” (’aql qodsî, intellectus sanctus), already established in Avicenna's philosophy, and the notion of the “angelic soul,” the faculty that receives prophecy in the psychology of the Brethren of Purity (Ikhwân al-Safâ’). These concepts are of fundamental importance.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01226

Here, as elsewhere, they form the foundation of “prophetic philosophy.” Thanks to them, mystical philosophers and speculative mystics can recognize a correspondence between two kinds of union: the union of the mystical sage with the Agent or Active Intelligence (’Aql fa’âl), understood as the Holy Spirit, and the union of the prophet's soul with the angelic Spirit, the Holy Spirit through whom Revelation actively takes place. In this way, the vocation of wisdom and mysticism can be brought into correspondence with the prophetic vocation.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01227

The same spiritual faculty can therefore be identified in the philosopher—or, more accurately, the theosopher—and in the prophet. This is the holy intellect, also called the holy spirit (rûh qodsîya) or holy faculty (qowwat qodsîya). These terms refer to the highest capacity of the human intellect: its ability to enter into frequent, habitual union with the Angel who is the “Active Intelligence,” and to receive directly from this angelic Spirit both intelligible truths and knowledge of spiritual realities generally, without requiring instruction from another human being.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01228

What distinguishes the prophet is the binding command to proclaim a message (risâla) before other people, in the case of the Nabî morsal, the prophet who is sent as a messenger; or initiation into the secret meaning of Revelation, in the case of the Nabî in the more general sense.
II. An Anonymous Treatise on the Seven Inner Meanings of the Qur'an
passage-en-01229

Yet the highest stage of philosophical knowledge, where philosophy culminates in mystical experience—as it does among the Ishrâqîyûn—leads the spiritual seeker through the same heavenly ascent (mi’râj) as the Nabî. Mystically, the seeker too becomes the “Seal of Prophecy.” The Angel of Knowledge is therefore none other than the Angel of Revelation. For this theosophy of the Holy Spirit, mystical religion and prophetic religion are not opposed. On the contrary, they find their shared fulfillment in a “prophetic philosophy,” because such a philosophy culminates in mystical experience. This experience is also individuation in its highest form. It takes place in the direct, one-to-one encounter between the philosopher and the Angel who is the Holy Spirit, without any human intermediary—not even a Church.
